messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Farah is a 59-year-old police officer, a married mother of two grown children, who had spent twenty-six years on the force without serious incident until a routine domestic-violence call in her precinct changed everything. The suspect, a large man high on methamphetamine, turned on her mid-interview, catching her off guard. He slammed her head against a kitchen counter, then kicked her repeatedly while screaming obscenities. She managed to call for backup, but by the time help arrived, she had been beaten unconscious. In the emergency room, she was treated for a concussion and facial fractures, but the internal damage was harder to chart. Within weeks, the sounds of that day—the man’s guttural yelling, the crack of her own skull against laminate—began replaying in her head with such sensory precision that she would wince and duck, certain she was hearing them for real. The terror she had felt in that kitchen came back in full force each time, her heart hammering as if the assault were happening again. After a memory hit, she would close her eyes and mentally recite the names of every street in her patrol sector, a self-taught ritual to shut the images down, but it meant she had to step away from whatever she was doing to do it alone. She started to believe that her body had turned against her, reacting to safety as though she were still under attack, and she grew convinced that she could not rely on anyone—not her partner, not her department, not the legal system—because the suspect had been released on bail the next day and no charges had stuck. What happened to her was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. And every time that sense of injustice rose, the memory of the beating would surface with it, as if her mind were demanding that she not forget what the world had allowed.

That sense of injustice colored everything. When her heart began to race, often for no apparent reason, she interpreted the pounding as proof that she was about to go crazy, and this triggered vivid, auditory-laced memories of the assault. The trigger of her own heartbeat thus brought back the same terror she had felt at the time. In turn, those memories reinforced her appraisal that her body was the enemy and that she could not trust the world to protect her. The more she remembered, the more hypervigilant she became, scanning every face in the station for potential threats. Driving with other people became especially difficult: if she had to take a cruiser with a partner, she would find herself watching every pedestrian, every oncoming car, certain that someone was about to attack, and her hypervigilance would make her heart race even faster, which then triggered more recall. The auditory component of the memory also made her sensitive to sudden noises, so a car backfiring or a raised voice in the precinct could send her back to that kitchen, her body reliving the blows. She began taking the stairs instead of the elevator to avoid the possibility of encountering a loud colleague, and she would leave the precinct before roll call to bypass the inevitable shouting.

To manage the distress, Farah began to employ strategies that only deepened the cycle. She isolated herself completely from friends and family, cutting off all contact because she could not bear the thought of relying on anyone who might fail her the way the system had. She also started monitoring her own thoughts constantly, terrified that any intrusive image meant she was losing her mind. This thought monitoring, however, made her more aware of her racing heart, which then triggered more memories. The isolation meant she had no distraction, so she spent hours alone with the vivid recall, which deepened her sense of injustice and reinforced her belief that others could not be trusted. Her hypervigilance towards people made even a casual encounter feel threatening, and she would avoid driving with others altogether, taking long routes alone or not going out at all. Being alone with her thoughts was not safe either; her memory would intrude, and the auditory recall seemed louder in silence. Each time she isolated herself, the memories became more frequent, as if she were giving them space to grow. The injustice she felt made her hyperaware of any sign of danger, turning ordinary situations into triggers, and her constant monitoring of her thoughts amplified her anxiety, so that her heart raced more easily.

Now, a year after the assault, Farah is seeking help because she can no longer function as a police officer; she has been assigned to desk duty, but even there she struggles, jumping at every phone call. Her marriage is strained because she refuses to drive anywhere with her husband and has stopped attending family gatherings. What she fears most is that she is indeed going crazy, and she hopes therapy can give her some control over her body and her mind, though she is deeply skeptical that anyone can truly understand what she endured or why she can no longer trust the world.
